lesson.title: The Non-Evolving Population: Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium as a Null Hypothesis
lesson.summary: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium describes the genotype frequencies expected in a population that is not evolving, and biologists use it as a baseline: when a real population's observed genotype frequencies deviate from that expectation, it signals that evolution is actually occurring.
lesson.body:
The last chapter calculated allele frequencies directly from observed genotype counts. Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium runs a related calculation in the other direction: starting from allele frequencies, it predicts what genotype frequencies should look like, under one specific, important condition, that the population is not evolving at that gene.

The model rests on five idealized conditions that together define a population where allele frequencies cannot change from one generation to the next: no new mutations arising, no migration of individuals, and their alleles, into or out of the population, an effectively infinite, or at least very large, population size so that chance alone does not shift frequencies between generations, completely random mating with no preference for or against particular genotypes, and no natural selection, meaning every genotype survives and reproduces equally well. If all five hold, the population's allele frequencies stay exactly the same generation after generation, and the population is, by the definition from two chapters back, not evolving at that locus.

Under those conditions, genotype frequencies follow directly from allele frequencies by simple probability, the same logic as a Punnett square, just applied to an entire population's gene pool instead of two parents. For a gene with two alleles, A with frequency p and a with frequency q, where p plus q equals 1, random mating means an offspring's two alleles are essentially drawn independently from that gene pool, one from the pool of sperm and one from the pool of eggs. The probability of drawing two A alleles is p times p, or p squared. The probability of drawing one A and one a is p times q, for an A from one parent and a from the other, plus q times p for the reverse combination, giving 2pq. The probability of drawing two a alleles is q times q, or q squared. Together, these must account for every possible offspring genotype, so p squared plus 2pq plus q squared equals 1.

A worked example shows how this gets used in practice. Suppose researchers survey a large population and find that 16 percent of individuals visibly express a particular trait caused by a fully recessive allele, meaning these individuals must be homozygous recessive, aa, at that gene, since a single dominant allele would mask the trait. That directly observed phenotype frequency gives q squared: q squared equals 0.16. Taking the square root gives q equals 0.4, the frequency of the recessive allele. Since p plus q equals 1, p equals 1 minus 0.4, which is 0.6, the frequency of the dominant allele. From here, the full set of expected genotype frequencies follows. Homozygous dominant, AA, is p squared, or 0.6 times 0.6, equaling 0.36, that is, 36 percent. Heterozygous, Aa, is 2pq, or 2 times 0.6 times 0.4, equaling 0.48, that is, 48 percent. Homozygous recessive, aa, is q squared, or 0.4 times 0.4, equaling 0.16, that is, 16 percent, which matches the originally observed value and confirms the arithmetic. As a final check, 0.36 plus 0.48 plus 0.16 equals 1.00. The practically useful result here is the 48 percent figure for heterozygous carriers. These individuals look phenotypically normal, since the trait is fully recessive and they carry only one copy of the recessive allele, and cannot be counted directly just by observation, yet the Hardy-Weinberg model lets researchers estimate how common they are in the population using only the directly observable frequency of the recessive phenotype.

The genuinely important point to take from this model is what it is actually for. No real population perfectly satisfies all five idealized conditions. Mutation always happens at some low rate, populations are never truly infinite, mating is rarely perfectly random, and selection is very often acting on at least some genes. Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, in other words, describes a population that, strictly speaking, does not exist in nature. That is not a flaw in the model, it is the whole point of building it. Because it precisely defines what genotype frequencies would look like if nothing were changing, biologists can calculate that expectation from a real population's measured allele frequencies, compare it to what is actually observed, and treat any meaningful mismatch as a signal that one or more of those five conditions is being violated, that is, that some real evolutionary process, mutation, migration, drift, non-random mating, or selection, is measurably at work in that population. A model built to describe a non-evolving population turns out, used this way, to be one of the sharpest available tools for detecting when evolution is actually happening.
